title: Researches in Sinai
venue: John Murray, London (Internet Archive scan); chapter 'The Foreign Writing', Serabit el-Khadim
ask_addressed: What is the documented lineage of writing systems: Egyptian hieroglyphs and Proto-Sinaitic to Phoenician to Greek to Latin and Cyrillic; cuneiform to Old Persian; Aramaic to Brahmi, Arabic and Hebrew scripts? Dates, inscriptions, and what is debated (e.g. Aramaic origin of Brahmi, independent invention of Chinese and Mesoamerican scripts).
summary: Petrie, who excavated Serabit el-Khadim, reports unreadable non-Egyptian inscriptions on a sphinx and about eight tablets, mixing a few hieroglyphs with other signs, and argues they are a definite writing system with repeated sign sequences. He does not say it descends from hieroglyphs.
limits: 1906 excavation report: pre-dates decipherment and the Wadi el-Hol finds; reports an observation of a separate system, not a derivation from hieroglyphs. Direct link to Phoenician is not argued.

strand.what: an apparently non-Egyptian sign system carved in Egyptian-style monuments by non-Egyptian miners

quote: It is a definite system, and not merely a scribbling made in ignorant imitation of Egyptian writing by men who knew no better.

title: Researches in Sinai
venue: John Murray, London (Internet Archive scan); chapter 'The Foreign Writing', Serabit el-Khadim
ask_addressed: Which links are documented by dated inscriptions and which are inferred from letter shapes?
summary: Petrie dates the Sinai writing to about 1500 BC from pottery, the sphinx and the Thutmose III-era stone, but treats it as one of many early alphabets, not as the single parent of the Phoenician alphabet.
limits: Petrie's wider theory of a deep-time common 'signary' (from 6000-7000 BC) is not accepted here as evidence. His 1500 BC date is superseded in later scholarship by earlier proposals (recalled, not fetched: Darnell et al. 2005 on Wadi el-Hol).

strand.what: whether the Sinai signs are the ancestor of the fixed Phoenician alphabet; Petrie says only one of several early alphabets

quote: one of the many alphabets which were in use in the Mediterranean lands long before the fixed alphabet selected by the Phoenicians

title: Herodotus, Histories, Book 5, chapter 58 (A. D. Godley translation)
ask_addressed: What is the documented lineage of writing systems: Egyptian hieroglyphs and Proto-Sinaitic to Phoenician to Greek to Latin and Cyrillic; cuneiform to Old Persian; Aramaic to Brahmi, Arabic and Hebrew scripts? Dates, inscriptions, and what is debated (e.g. Aramaic origin of Brahmi, independent invention of Chinese and Mesoamerican scripts).
summary: Herodotus (writing in the 5th century BC) says Phoenicians who came with Cadmus brought the alphabet to Hellas and that Ionians learned it from them, calling the letters 'Phoenician'.
limits: A literary tradition with a legendary founder (Cadmus), not an inscription; gives no date. Evidence for the Greek borrowing rests on letter shapes, order and names, not on this text.

strand.what: the alphabet, as remembered in Greek tradition

quote: brought with them to Hellas, among many other kinds of learning, the alphabet, which had been unknown before this, I think, to the Greeks

title: Greek Writing from Knossos to Homer: A Linguistic Interpretation of the Origin of the Greek Alphabet and the Continuity of Ancient Greek Literacy
venue: Cambridge University Press 1997 (Internet Archive scan); chapter 6 'Phoenician Beginnings'
ask_addressed: Which links are documented by dated inscriptions and which are inferred from letter shapes?
summary: Woodard states the Greeks 'unquestionably' acquired the alphabet from Semitic-speaking users of a consonantal Canaanite script and, citing McCarter, gives three grounds: letter forms, near-identical letter order, and Semitic-derived letter names.
limits: The case is typological (shape, order, names), not a dated inscription recording the handover. Woodard himself disputes where and when.

strand.what: consonantal letters adapted as the Greek alphabet; shared letter order and names

quote: the characters of the most archaic Greek scripts closely match those of the Phoenician script

summary: Woodard accepts the Phoenician source but argues the adapters were already literate in the Cypriot syllabary and that Cyprus was the place of origin, noting 'considerable disagreement' on where, when and why the script reached the Aegean.
limits: A single author's minority-leaning thesis; useful mainly as proof that place, date and agency of the Phoenician-to-Greek step are contested while the source script is not.

strand.what: place and agency of the adaptation (Cypriot scribes) rather than the Phoenician source

quote: one alphabetic foot also rests on a shoulder of the syllabic script of the Cypriot Greeks

title: The Local Scripts of Archaic Greece: A Study of the Origin of the Greek Alphabet and Its Development from the Eighth to the Fifth Centuries B.C.
authors: Jeffery, L. H.; Johnston, A. W. (rev.)
venue: Oxford: Clarendon Press, revised edition with supplement by A. W. Johnston, 1990 (Internet Archive scan); chapter on the origin of the Greek alphabet
ask_addressed: Which links are documented by dated inscriptions and which are inferred from letter shapes?
summary: Jeffery's standard epigraphic study frames the date of the Greek alphabet as disputed over seven centuries, then argues from Semitic letter forms (tailed kaph, tailless dalet) for a date after the ninth century BC, with the Dipylon oinochoe as an early Attic text.
limits: Dating rests on comparing letter forms with Semitic inscriptions, so it is inference, not a dated transfer record. Later work (including Woodard) pushes the question further.

strand.what: date of adoption, bounded below by Semitic letter forms and above by the earliest Greek inscriptions (Dipylon, c. 740 BC)

quote: The dispute concerning this date has ranged over seven centuries—from the fourteenth to the late eighth.

summary: Jeffery treats the Greek-to-Etruscan-to-Roman chain as established background to her argument, mentioning contact between Etruscans and 'the Greeks of Kyme'.
limits: Passing statement in an argument about Greek origins, not a dedicated treatment of the Latin alphabet; no inscription dates given in the passage.

strand.what: Greek letters passed to Etruscans and then to Romans

quote: the Etruscan learners of the Greek alphabet

title: The Alphabet: An Account of the Origin and Development of Letters
venue: Kegan Paul, Trench & Co., London (Internet Archive scan)
ask_addressed: What is the documented lineage of writing systems: Egyptian hieroglyphs and Proto-Sinaitic to Phoenician to Greek to Latin and Cyrillic; cuneiform to Old Persian; Aramaic to Brahmi, Arabic and Hebrew scripts? Dates, inscriptions, and what is debated (e.g. Aramaic origin of Brahmi, independent invention of Chinese and Mesoamerican scripts).
summary: Taylor derives the Latin alphabet via the Chalcidian variety of the archaic Greek alphabet carried by Chalcidian colonies to Cumae and Neapolis in Italy, and dates the earliest Greek inscriptions to perhaps the 8th-9th century BC.
limits: 1883 synthesis: dates and the Etruscan intermediary have been refined since. Inference from letter forms and colonial geography, not a dated handover.

strand.what: Chalcidian letter forms carried by colonists in Italy

quote: colonies from Chalcis, which were established in Sicily, and also in central Italy at Cumae and Neapolis

title: The Alphabet: An Account of the Origin and Development of Letters
venue: Kegan Paul, Trench & Co., London (Internet Archive scan)
ask_addressed: What is the documented lineage of writing systems: Egyptian hieroglyphs and Proto-Sinaitic to Phoenician to Greek to Latin and Cyrillic; cuneiform to Old Persian; Aramaic to Brahmi, Arabic and Hebrew scripts? summary: Taylor states the Russian (Cyrillic) letters were borrowed from Greek in the 9th century and renamed in Slavonic, citing it as an analogy for the renaming of Phoenician letters in Greek.
limits: Incidental remark, not an analysis of Cyrillic. Silent on Glagolitic and on the Preslav origin of Cyrillic; the Cyril-Methodius and Glagolitic questions are NOT covered by any opened source (see Gaps).

strand.what: Greek letter forms adapted for Slavonic, with letters renamed

quote: The Russian letters, which were borrowed in the 9th century from the Greek alphabet, have lost the familiar Greek appellations

title: The Sculptures and Inscription of Darius the Great on the Rock of Behistun in Persia: a new collation of the Persian, Susian and Babylonian texts
authors: King, L. W.; Thompson, R. C.
venue: British Museum, London (Internet Archive scan); Epigraph L, Susian version
ask_addressed: What is the documented lineage of writing systems: Egyptian hieroglyphs and Proto-Sinaitic to Phoenician to Greek to Latin and Cyrillic; cuneiform to Old Persian; Aramaic to Brahmi, Arabic and Hebrew scripts? Dates, inscriptions, and what is debated (e.g. Aramaic origin of Brahmi, independent invention of Chinese and Mesoamerican scripts).
summary: The standard 1907 collation prints a trilingual royal inscription of Darius I (Old Persian, Susian/Elamite, Babylonian) and, in the Susian-only Epigraph L, a fragmentary statement that Darius made inscriptions 'in another fashion ... such as was not formerly' and sent copies into all lands.
limits: The English reconstruction is fragmentary and the passage in this edition does not name the script; it supports a Darius-era date (c. 520 BC) for Old Persian writing but not by itself the derivation from Mesopotamian cuneiform, which is inferred from sign structure. Whether texts attributed to Cyrus or Ariaramnes are earlier is disputed.

strand.what: a simplified, semi-alphabetic cuneiform script attested first under Darius I at Behistun

quote: By the grace of Auramazda I made inscriptions in another fashion

title: On the Origin of the Indian Brahma Alphabet
venue: Trubner, London / Indian Studies No. III (Internet Archive scan); translation of 1895 German original
ask_addressed: Which links are documented by dated inscriptions and which are inferred from letter shapes?
summary: Buhler argues that Kharosthi, the right-to-left script of Ashoka's north-western edicts (Shahbazgarhi, Mansehra), derives from the Aramaic of the Achaemenid empire, introduced by Darius's satrapal administration, and cites the Old Persian word dipi in the Indian edicts.
limits: Argument from letter forms and imperial administration; the pre-Achaemenid conquest is called 'doubtful and disputed'. 19th-century work, since supplemented by Aramaic Ashokan inscriptions (not opened here).

strand.what: Aramaic chancery letters adapted for Prakrit

quote: the introduction of the Aramaean letters into the Indian province could only date from the reign of Darius

title: On the Origin of the Indian Brahma Alphabet
venue: Trubner, London / Indian Studies No. III (Internet Archive scan); translation of 1895 German original
ask_addressed: What is the documented lineage of writing systems: Egyptian hieroglyphs and Proto-Sinaitic to Phoenician to Greek to Latin and Cyrillic; cuneiform to Old Persian; Aramaic to Brahmi, Arabic and Hebrew scripts? Dates, inscriptions, and what is debated (e.g. Aramaic origin of Brahmi, independent invention of Chinese and Mesoamerican scripts).
summary: Buhler lists five competing derivations of Brahmi, then argues for a North Semitic (Phoenician/Aramaic-type) source imported by traders around 800 BC, long before Ashoka's securely dated edicts of the 3rd century BC.
limits: Dated by comparing letter shapes with Mesha stone and Assyrian weights; no Indian inscription of that age is cited. This early date and the Semitic origin itself remain contested (see Cunningham; Falk and Salomon recalled, not fetched).

strand.what: prototypes of the Brahmi letters, dated by Buhler to c. 800 BC

quote: this period must fall somewhere between circiter 890 and 750 B. C.

title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. I: Inscriptions of Asoka
venue: Office of the Superintendent of Government Printing, Calcutta (Internet Archive scan); plate and essay 'Origin of the Indian Alphabet'
ask_addressed: What is the documented lineage of writing systems: Egyptian hieroglyphs and Proto-Sinaitic to Phoenician to Greek to Latin and Cyrillic; cuneiform to Old Persian; Aramaic to Brahmi, Arabic and Hebrew scripts? Dates, inscriptions, and what is debated (e.g. Aramaic origin of Brahmi, independent invention of Chinese and Mesoamerican scripts).
summary: The survey officer who edited the Ashokan edicts rejects a Semitic or Phoenician origin for the Indian (Brahmi) alphabet and argues it was an indigenous invention, while admitting the Shahbazgarhi (Kharosthi) script is Semitic in character.
limits: Printed 1879 (title page); OCR of the scan corrupts some letters, so the quotation is normalised for OCR homoglyphs. Pre-dates all modern dating evidence; reasoning is from letter forms. The indigenous theory is not the current majority view but is revived in modified form by recent authors (recalled, not fetched: Falk 2018).

strand.what: Cunningham denies any borrowing: Brahmi as independent Indian invention

quote: the Indian alphabet is of purely Indian origin, just as much as the Egyptian hieroglyphics were the purely local invention of the people of Egypt

title: Western Mesoamerican Calendars and Writing Systems (ch. 3: The Writing System of Epiclassic Central Mexico, by Helmke, C. and Nielsen, J.)
ask_addressed: What is the documented lineage of writing systems: Egyptian hieroglyphs and Proto-Sinaitic to Phoenician to Greek to Latin and Cyrillic; cuneiform to Old Persian; Aramaic to Brahmi, Arabic and Hebrew scripts? Dates, inscriptions, and what is debated (e.g. Aramaic origin of Brahmi, independent invention of Chinese and Mesoamerican scripts).
summary: The chapter reasons that the shared features of Mesoamerican scripts (Epiclassic, Teotihuacan and others) point to descent from one earliest Mesoamerican writing system, citing Rodriguez Martinez et al. 2006 (Cascajal) among others; the volume's introduction notes nearly a dozen systems, most undeciphered.
limits: Addresses descent within Mesoamerica, not independence from Old World scripts (that is assumed, not tested). It does not give a date for the first writing; the Cascajal Block's date is disputed (not opened). No Chinese source was opened.

strand.from: Earliest Mesoamerican writing (Olmec/Cascajal horizon, cited not opened)
strand.to: Teotihuacan, Epiclassic and later Mesoamerican scripts
strand.what: a regional tradition descending from one early script, with no documented Old World source

quote: imply a common descent from the earliest writing system developed in Mesoamerica
